title: Survey Myths That Harm UX
intro: Surveys are fast, scalable and look great on a slide, which is why they get asked to do jobs they can't.

learn.title: Five myths
learn.text:
**“Surveys tell you what users do”** → they tell you what users *say*.
**“75% of users prefer A”** → 75% of 28 respondents did.
**“A survey can validate an idea”** → predicting future use is unreliable.
**“Self-rated 'easy' means easy”** → users rate failed tasks as easy.
**“Always run a standard survey”** → pick the instrument for the question.

try.q: How should you report a survey result?
options: As a percentage of the user base
As a trend against last quarter

learn.title: The say–do gap, measured
learn.text:
“Ask 100 people how often they exercise, then compare with gym check-ins.” The gap is the same in UX.

Calabro has watched hundreds of moderated sessions where participants struggle, hesitate and use trial and error — then say the task was easy.

A user reports using a feature “frequently”; analytics show twice in six months.

try.q: A participant struggles visibly, then rates the task easy. What does that tell you?
options: The task was easier than it looked
The rating scale was badly worded
The participant only wanted to be polite about it
try.explain: It is a consistent pattern across hundreds of sessions.

learn.title: What surveys are good at
learn.text:
Attitudes, preferences, self-reported context and satisfaction trends over time — measured honestly, with the right instrument.

What they can't do: tell you what happened, or confirm that an idea will work. For those, watch behaviour or run a test.

try.q: Which question is a survey well suited to?
options: How confident do people feel about this?
How long does the task take?
Where exactly do users abandon the checkout flow?
Which design is faster to use?
try.explain: Attitudes and self-reported context — not behaviour.

test.explain: Which is useful, as long as you don't claim otherwise. Remember or want to believe.

test.q: Why can't a survey validate an idea?
options: Predicting your own future use is unreliable
Respondents rarely read the questions carefully
test.explain: Intent is a weak predictor of behaviour.

test.q: What's wrong with “75% of users prefer A”?
options: Respondents aren't the whole user base
The percentage needs a confidence interval

test.q: When is a standardised survey the wrong choice?
options: When the question needs a different instrument
When stakeholders simply want a number to report
test.explain: Pick the instrument for the question, not out of habit.

test.q: What is the exercise-and-gym-check-ins example for?
test.explain: The same gap applies in UX.
